content: Diphtheritic stomatitis is a newly identified disease that has so far been observed exclusively in Yellow-eyed penguins (Megadyptes antipodes). The clinical presentation of this condition resembles human diphtheria, with the hallmark being infectious lesions in the oral cavity. These lesions interfere with the ability to swallow and can lead to respiratory complications. The causative agent of the disease is Corynebacterium amycolatum, an aerobic, Gram-positive bacterium. The disease predominantly affects very young chicks. However, it is hypothesized that an additional factor, such as a viral agent, may act as a precursor, enabling the corynebacterium to function as a secondary pathogen. This disease has been a significant contributor to mortality during the Yellow-eyed penguin breeding seasons of 2002 and 2004. The outbreaks appear to have been geographically restricted to the South Island of New Zealand and Stewart Island/Rakiura. The clinical signs and symptoms of diphtheritic stomatitis are primarily observed in Yellow-eyed penguin chicks. Affected individuals exhibit labored breathing and generalized weakness. A yellow, caseous exudate is often visible within the beak and at the corners of the mouth. A yellow diphtheritic membrane typically forms, covering the hard palate, tongue, and buccal mucosa. In severe cases, the lesions prevent the mouth from closing properly, and the tongue may remain exposed. The diagnosis of diphtheritic stomatitis can be confirmed through two primary methods: the isolation of Corynebacterium amycolatum from a clinical specimen or a histopathological examination that identifies features consistent with diphtheria. During the 2004 outbreak, various treatment strategies were explored. The primary approach involved the administration of antibiotics. The outcomes of these treatments varied significantly. The efficacy of antibiotic therapy, particularly when applied to wild populations, remains a topic of ongoing discussion and debate among experts. This information has been summarized from the proceedings of the Yellow-eyed Penguin Corynebacterium Workshop, which took place in Dunedin on Tuesday, April 5, 2005.
